Staples: Assortment Gap & Recommendation Analysis - Archetype

The question

Staples wants to grow its marketplace with core-adjacent products: design and lifestyle extensions of things it already sells (the “White Chair” idea: an aesthetic-first chair next to Staples' ergonomic range), without taking sales from its own first-party assortment. Using only external data, this PoC compares each granular Staples shelf with a competitor's range and asks:

  • Where are the gaps? Which archetypes and attribute values (colour, material, style, price band, features) are more common at the competitor than at Staples?
  • Are they safe and on-brand? Would a product take a sale from a Staples item, does it fit Staples' customer, and is it priced to trade up or to undercut?
  • What should be added? Named archetypes with example products and notes on brands and sellers.

How we approached it

Four phases: make the comparison fair, describe every product the same way, score each archetype two ways, then decide.

1 · Make the comparison fair
S0

Ingest & clean

Load both retailers' product files and clean them so every later stage reads the same fields.

OutputClean product tables for both retailers
Techpandas · PyArrow · ftfy · regex · Python ast

Group Staples colour-variant SKUs into one family so both retailers are counted the same way.

Use Staples' own leaf categories as shelves, splitting large ones by Staples' product-type facet.

The two methods

Each method keeps its own final score. Neither is blended into the other; they meet only in the final ranking.

Method 1 · vector view → VOS

Every product becomes a “card” (same template on both sides: type, colour, material, style, features, vibe, use; no price) and is embedded with BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5.

VW
Vector Whitespace: how few Staples products sit near this product, after balancing sample sizes.
AAS
Fit with Staples: closeness to Staples' catalogue on this L2 plus overlap with the use contexts Staples serves.
CRS
Cannibalisation risk: functional similarity to the nearest Staples products. Ignores price and looks by design.
AD
Aesthetic delta: how different the colour, material, style and vibe are from the nearest Staples product.
PPR
Price ratio to the nearest Staples products. Used only in the labels, never in a score.

VOS = 100 × [0.45·pct(VW) + 0.3·AAS/100 + 0.25·pct(AD)] × (1 − CRS/100)

Method 2 · attribute view → TG

Archetypes are compared as shares of each retailer's shelf, so a sample is compared with a sample, never with a census.

LSR
Log share ratio: how over-represented the archetype is at the competitor. Defined even when Staples has none; shrunk when not statistically credible.
PPG
Price position gap: distance between the two price distributions (↑ = competitor priced higher).
CG
Colour gap: difference in colour-tone mix.
MSG
Material & style gap.
DFG
Design-forward gap: competitor median DFI minus Staples median DFI.

TG = 100 × [0.35·pct(LSR) + 0.2·pct(PPG) + 0.15·pct(CG) + 0.15·pct(MSG) + 0.15·pct(DFG)]

From two scores to one list

  1. Safety gate (shared by both methods). An archetype qualifies only if:
    • at least 50% of its competitor products are approvable (CURATE, STYLE-EXTENSION or TRADE-UP), and
    • fewer than 30% would substitute or undercut a Staples product.
    It applies to both scores because TG alone cannot see cannibalisation.
  2. Fused re-rank. Within each shelf, VOS and TG are turned into percentile ranks and combined: Final = 0.5·rank(VOS) + 0.5·rank(TG). Using ranks stops either score's scale from dominating.
  3. Agreement tier. Each archetype is placed in a tier by where it sits in each method's ranking:
    • Strong: top third in both methods.
    • Gap-led: top third on TG only (a real attribute gap that the vector view finds crowded or close to Staples).
    • Vector-led: top third on VOS only (whitespace the attribute grid does not capture).
    • Weak: top third in neither; never recommended.
  4. Shortlist. Up to 5 non-Weak archetypes per shelf, in Final order.
  5. Robustness check. Both sets of weights are re-drawn 1,000 times; the report shows how often each archetype stays in its shelf's top 5.

Assumptions and caveats

  • Provisional PoC run. Attributes come from the local rules + embedding instrument (no LLM key available); style, vibe tags and the Design-Forward Index still need human validation; thresholds are weakly supervised, not yet calibrated with Pat.
  • All figures are shares within a convenience sample, never absolute market sizes.
  • The competitor is chosen per shelf. In this run every shelf is compared with Wayfair, the only competitor with product-level data so far.
  • Everything Staples.com sells counts as existing assortment for cannibalisation, including third-party brands it retails.
  • The competitor data is a convenience sample (pages that scraped successfully). Every number is a within-sample share with a credibility check; nothing here estimates market size or demand.
  • Competitor consumer and professional (B2B) pages are pooled. Prices are list prices at crawl time.
  • The competitor's “vendor” is often a house brand, not a manufacturer: those products are recommendations to source the archetype, not to recruit that brand.
  • Category-specific vocabularies, the page crosswalk and the house-brand list are drafts awaiting review. Shelves in L2s without a reviewed configuration are marked provisional.
Showing 8 of 23 shelves: how they were chosen

To keep the report focused, Chairs & Seating is limited to 5 shelves and Desks is limited to 3 shelves. Categories added later show every shelf. All shelves are still scored and listed in outputs/tables/shelf_selection.csv.

  1. R1 Enough data (required): at least 30 product families on each side.
  2. R2 Meaningful recommendations (required): at least one archetype recommended.
  3. R3 Reliable placement: ≥ 85% of mapped competitor products placed with high confidence.
  4. R4 Methods agree: Spearman VOS↔TG ≥ 0.30.
  5. R5 Backed by both methods: at least 1 Strong-tier recommendation.

Shelves meeting R1–R2 are ranked by how many of R3–R5 they pass, then by number of recommendations, then by agreement.

Key insights

Price
  • Median price: Wayfair $350 vs Staples $394.
  • Price gap in under $200: Wayfair 22% of its range vs Staples 16% (credible).
Where Wayfair is deeper (credible gaps)
  • Back height “high”: Wayfair 67% vs Staples 10%.
  • Form factor “accent”: Wayfair 58% vs Staples 12%.
  • Use context “residential living”: Wayfair 36% vs Staples 7%.
Where Staples is deeper (not a gap)
  • Key benefits “commercial-grade”: Staples 64% vs Wayfair 7%.
  • Back height “mid”: Staples 80% vs Wayfair 25%.
Design
  • Design-forward share (DFI ≥ 0.6): Wayfair 77% vs Staples 18%.
Recommendation
  • Top pick: Mid-century — warm neutral, $200–$350 (Strong agreement); 57% of its Wayfair products are safe to add.
  • Safe to add: 416 of 1,064 Wayfair products (0 CURATE, 242 STYLE-EXTENSION, 174 TRADE-UP).
  • Would cannibalise: 382 Wayfair products would substitute or undercut a Staples item.
  • Quick-win sellers: 2 brand(s) behind recommended products already sell on Staples.
